They're all against net neutrality laws. But some are for net neutrality and some are against it.

A lot of it has to do with not wanting more government control of the internet and setting a precedent that the government should have that much control. It also just hasn't been needed for the past 20 years, so there's really not much reason to think it is now. The reason the internet has seen so much innovation is almost entirely because of the few regulations on it. If you want to start a new social network, or an online store, or build an app, you can basically sit down, try it, and succeed or fail. Try that in any of the highly regulated fields (energy, finance, medicine), and you have to spend tens of millions or billions to even begin to do anything innovative in those fields. Regulation is what is holding these fields back, and a lot of us don't want to see the same thing happen to the internet.

The reclassification that took place in February has nothing to do with innovation. If anything it's keeping the door for innovation open. Prior to this, if a small startup began offering a service that (in an ISP's opinion) was sending too much data to their customers they could decide to hold them hostage and force them to pay extra to deliver my content to my customers in spite of the fact that my customers are already paying them to access my content. A small startup wouldn't be able to handle this and would have to fold. Their innovation would be dead.

The poster boy for this is of course Netflix, who is big enough to handle the fees apparently, but before Title II there would have been nothing stopping (for example) Comcast or Time Warner from doing the same thing to a company that was trying to compete with one of the subsidiaries or sister companies in their giant conglomerates. ISP's shouldn't have any hand in what information is transmitted - they're just a conduit.

In an ideal world none of this regulation would be necessary, but when ISP's start slowing down my access to sites and services in spite of the fact that I am paying them for access it's just bullshit. Their business practices brought this on themselves. If they were in the habit of innovating prices and speeds would be going down, not up, and I wouldn't have trouble streaming YouTube when I'm paying for a 50Mbps connection.

I'm thinking of taxes allotted for funding of education, welfare, health programs, and other social programs funded by the state.

For example, Mississippi (last I checked) was the most obese state in the nation, and they had the highest bang for your buck on this map, leading me to think that maybe they're spending less in health programs than others state, therefore taking in less taxes overall, resulting in more money in a person's pocket. If there's more money in a person's pocket, businesses don't have to charge as much to get consumers to buy just as much.

This could also be a correlation =/= causation thing too, but it's interesting to see. I honestly don't know enough about this topic to say, and if you were willing and able to put forth the research, I would be grateful.

I'll pick one random state with a higher relative value and one just below average, so Mississippi and Colorado. This will be very un-scientific-y and just some comparisons to try to get a better idea.

Just basing it off of income, sales, and property taxes, MS has a max of 5% income tax (at $10k), an average sales tax of 7%, and a .52% property tax. Colorado has a 4.63% flat income tax, and average sales tax of 7.39%, and a property tax of .6%. Colorado has 5.3 million people with a median income of around $57k while Mississippi has 3 million people with a median income of $36k.

The sales taxes aren't all that different, but just by eyeballing it, Colorado pulls in way more in taxes based on the higher median income and population, and way more on property taxes with the much higher property values. They would also probably pull in more from sales taxes because there are more people living there to buy stuff and it also has a large tourism industry which would bring in people to buy stuff.

The most recent data on spending from 2012 has MS spending $27.8 billion on welfare programs and CO spending $49.1 Billion, which means Colorado spends roughly $9,500 per person and Mississippi spends roughly $9,300 per person. So it works out to pretty equal in money spent on welfare per person. I think it more has to do with the overall population and demand for property in the states that drives the relative value up or down. Colorado is a place where people want to be so the higher demand causes property value to rise which means stores have to charge more to cover their own property expenses and more expensive employee salaries. Mississippi just has a much lower demand.

There obviously are way more variables that affect all of these things but I thought the comparisons were at least interesting.
